title: Wire crochet
subtitle: Crocheting with craft wire to make jewellery and rigid decorative structures
excerpt: Wire crochet is the technique of crocheting with fine craft wire instead of yarn. The hook is the same; the wire holds its shape instead of returning to rest. You can make rings, pendants, bangles, and small sculptural forms that hold their structure without any stiffening treatment.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing). Contemporary jewellery-making technique references, public domain tool guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: Crocheting with fine craft wire rather than yarn. The stitches are formed in the same way, but the wire holds its shape permanently rather than springing back to a relaxed state.
A coiled, spring-steel wire that returns to its coil shape after distortion. Used in jewellery-making for bangles and necklaces that require no clasp.

content.text: uses fine craft wire in place of yarn to produce small rigid forms. The stitches are the same as standard crochet: chain, double crochet (UK), slip stitch. The difference is that wire holds the shape you give it, rather than relaxing back to a natural drape. A wire crochet ring stays round; a yarn crochet ring does not.

The most common materials are 0.3 mm and 0.4 mm craft wire in copper, silver-plated, or coloured aluminium. Copper is the easiest to work; it is soft, bends readily, and can be shaped with your fingers as well as the hook. Wire is sold in reels; a standard 10 m reel makes several small pieces.

items.name: Fine craft wire, 0.3 mm or 0.4 mm
items.note: Copper is easiest for beginners. Silver-plate is more expensive but tarnishes less.

items.name: Steel crochet hook, 0.75 mm or 1.0 mm
items.note: Use a steel hook rather than aluminium. Wire can scratch and burr the shaft of a soft metal hook.

items.name: Wire cutters or sturdy scissors
items.note: Household scissors will be damaged by repeated wire cutting. Use dedicated wire cutters.

items.name: Round-nose pliers
items.note: For closing jump rings and forming small loops at finished ends

content.text: Wire does not slip off the hook the way yarn does, but it also does not slide along the hook as smoothly. Work each stitch a little more loosely than you would with yarn. If the loops are too tight, the hook becomes difficult to insert for the next stitch and the wire can kink at the stitch top.
Leave a 10 cm tail of wire. Form a slip knot in the usual way, but hold it loosely. Wire will not tighten and release the way yarn does, so the slip knot is more of a holding loop.
Work a foundation chain of the required length. Keep the loops slightly larger than you think you need. Wire chains can close down as you work across them.

Work rows or rounds in double crochet (UK). Insert the hook, wrap the wire around the hook from back to front in the usual yarn-over motion, and draw a loop through. The wire holds each loop as you make it.

To fasten off, cut the wire leaving a 5 cm tail. Thread the tail through the last stitch with round-nose pliers if needed, and tuck it back through two or three stitches on the wrong side. Squeeze the end flat with the pliers so it does not catch.

Memory wire is too rigid to work with a hook directly. Make a length of crocheted copper wire first, then thread it onto the memory wire loop. The result is a textured bangle that holds its round shape.

is too hard to crochet with directly, but a length of crocheted 0.3 mm wire can be threaded onto a memory wire bangle loop after it is made, forming a textured bangle that retains its circular shape without a clasp.

items.symptom: The wire kinks sharply at a stitch point and will not lie flat
items.cause: The loop was pulled too tight when completing the stitch, or the hook was inserted at an angle that bent the wire against itself.
items.fix: Very fine kinks can be pressed gently with your thumbnail against a flat surface. Larger kinks are permanent. Cut the wire at the kink point and restart from the last undamaged stitch, leaving a long enough tail to secure later.

items.symptom: The hook keeps catching in the stitches
items.cause: The loops are too small, or the wire is slightly burred from the cut end.
items.fix: Work the stitches more loosely. File any burr off the cut end of the wire with a small metal file before starting.

items.symptom: The finished piece distorts when handled
items.cause: Very fine wire (0.2 mm or below) does not hold its shape well under repeated handling.
items.fix: Use 0.3 mm minimum for anything that will be worn or handled. Reserve 0.2 mm for purely decorative or framed pieces.

content.text: A small flat circle in double crochet (UK) worked in the round from a magic ring is the standard wire crochet starter piece. Work 6 rounds in 0.3 mm copper wire at a 1.0 mm hook. The result is a firm disc about 3 cm across that can be used as a pendant, a button, or a decorative patch.
